summary: Extends the Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC) base solution from RFC 7683 with a new overload abatement algorithm. It lets an overloaded node set a maximum rate at which others may send it Diameter requests. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A busy shop can tell customers to send at most so many orders per minute. This is how a Diameter server says its limit.

questions: what is diameter overload rate control
subtitle: How an overloaded Diameter node can cap the number of requests per second that other nodes send it.

tldr.problem: The default Diameter overload method asks senders to drop a percentage of requests, which copes badly when the offered load changes quickly: a spike still pushes too much traffic through.
tldr.mechanism: A new rate algorithm lets the overloaded node name a maximum number of requests per second in a new OC-Maximum-Rate AVP, and senders hold their traffic to that rate, for example with a leaky bucket.
tldr.outcome: The overloaded node gets a fixed ceiling on its load regardless of how much work the senders receive, at the cost of tracking and dividing the rate among each sender. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Rate of zero
facts.value: No traffic is to be sent

today: RFC 8582 is a Proposed Standard from August 2019, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7683 and works with the peer report type of RFC 8581.

sections.title: Why a Percentage Is Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 8582 extends the Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC) solution from RFC 7683. DOIC's default loss algorithm tells a sending node to abate (divert or throttle) a percentage of its requests. The RFC argues this reacts poorly to changing load: it throttles too much during a dip and not enough during a spike.

The RFC's worked example: a sender handles 100 service requests per second and is told to cut 10%, so it sends 90. If its load jumps to 1000 per second it keeps cutting only 10% and sends 900. The overloaded node could ask for a 91% cut, but once the spike ends that would leave just 9 requests per second, so another report is needed. This feedback loop can cause wide swings in traffic.

With the rate algorithm the overloaded node instead says 'at most 90 requests per second', and the sender sends 90 whether it sees 100 or 1000 service requests per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling a shop to turn away one customer in ten does not help when a crowd shows up. Telling it 'serve only 90 an hour' works whether the crowd is small or huge.

sections.title: Reporting Nodes and Reacting Nodes
sections.content:
A reporting node is a DOIC node that sends an Overload report in a Diameter answer message. A reacting node is a DOIC node that receives and acts on such a report. The rate algorithm can be selected for all three DOIC report types: HOST_REPORT (0), REALM_REPORT (1) and PEER_REPORT (2, from RFC 8581).

The RFC notes that the rate approach has a consequence: the reporting node must decide how to share its capacity among its reacting nodes. With a capacity of 100 transactions per second and 10 reacting nodes, it could give each 10. It could also give one high-capacity node 55 and each of the other 9 nodes 5. So the reporting node has to keep state for each reacting node and redistribute the rate when nodes are added, removed or fail.
sections.plainLanguage: If a pizza shop can make 100 pizzas an hour and ten offices order, it has to decide how many each office may order, and change the split if an office joins or leaves.

sections.title: Announcing and Selecting the Algorithm
sections.content:
Support for the rate feature is announced with a new bit in the OC-Feature-Vector AVP. Because every DOIC node must support the loss algorithm, a node that supports rate supports both. A reacting node that supports rate MUST indicate both loss and rate in its OC-Feature-Vector.

The reporting node picks a single algorithm and reports its choice in the answer. For Host and Realm reports the choice is in the OC-Feature-Vector AVP, and for Peer reports it is in the OC-Peer-Algo AVP. A reporting node can pick one algorithm for Host and Realm reports and a different one for Peer reports.

The new feature bit is OLR_RATE_ALGORITHM with the value 0x0000000000000004.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides first say which rules they know. The busy side then picks one set of rules for everyone to follow.

sections.title: Overload Report Handling
sections.content:
A reporting node using the rate algorithm SHOULD keep Overload Control State (OCS) for each reacting node it sends a rate report to. This differs from RFC 7683, where one loss percentage goes to all. An entry is identified by Application-ID, report type and the DiameterIdentity of the target, and it should include the rate allocated to that node. For Host reports the target comes from Origin-Host, for Realm reports from Origin-Realm, and for Peer reports it is the peer the request came from.

When sending a rate report, the reporting node MUST include the OC-Maximum-Rate AVP in the OC-OLR AVP and MUST NOT include OC-Reduction-Percentage. It may also send rate reports while not overloaded, as a way to avoid overload; that is left to local policy.

A reacting node saves the received rate in its own OCS entry. It can use the algorithm in the RFC's Section 8 or any other that correctly limits the maximum rate. Requests chosen for abatement are then throttled or diverted using the procedures of RFC 7683 and RFC 8581.
sections.plainLanguage: The busy side keeps a note of what limit it gave each sender. Each sender writes down its own limit and keeps to it.

sections.title: The OC-Maximum-Rate AVP
sections.content:
The extension adds one optional field, OC-Maximum-Rate, to the OC-OLR AVP (AVP header code 623). It has AVP code 670, type Unsigned32, and gives the maximum rate the receiver is asked to send, in requests per second. A value of zero means no traffic is to be sent. The AVP flag rules say the V bit MUST NOT be set.

No new report types are defined. The existing HOST_REPORT, REALM_REPORT and PEER_REPORT types all apply to the rate algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one number in the message: how many requests per second you may send. Zero means please send nothing.

sections.title: The Leaky Bucket Reference Algorithm
sections.content:
How the reporting node estimates its overload and picks a target rate is out of scope. It MUST evaluate this periodically and give each reacting node a share of the target. The maximum rate covers the whole stream of requests from that node, even if priority means only some are abated. The rate is a loose upper bound, and the combined load should converge towards the target or lower.

For the reacting node the RFC gives a reference leaky bucket algorithm based on ITU-T I.371. Set T = 1 / OC-Maximum-Rate. The bucket counter X drains at one unit per unit of time and grows by T for each forwarded request. On each new request, compute Xp = X - (ta - LCT). If Xp is at most the tolerance TAU, forward the request and set X = max(0, Xp) + T and LCT = ta. Otherwise apply abatement and leave X and LCT unchanged. The RFC suggests TAU = 4*T as a compromise between burst size and adaptation at low offered rate.

If OC-Maximum-Rate is 0 with a non-zero OC-Validity-Duration, abate 100% of requests. If OC-Validity-Duration is 0, stop abating.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a bucket with a small hole. Each request pours a little water in, and the water drips out at a steady pace. If the bucket is too full, you hold the request back.

sections.title: Priorities and Avoiding Resonance
sections.content:
For priority traffic the RFC adds a second threshold. With TAU1 < TAU2, all requests are admitted when the bucket is at or below TAU1, only higher-priority requests when it is between TAU1 and TAU2, and none above TAU2. This generalizes to n priorities with n thresholds. Reasonable values given are TAU0 = 0, TAU1 = 1/2 * TAU2 and TAU2 = 10 * T.

The RFC also describes an optional fix for resonance: if many senders start at once, their buckets can fall into step and send batched, peaky arrivals. Randomizing the bucket increment avoids this. When the bucket has emptied, add T + uT where u is uniform between -1/2 and +1/2, and apply the same randomization when control is activated. At high load randomization rarely occurs, so the admitted rate stays precise.
sections.plainLanguage: Important requests get a slightly bigger bucket so they still get through. And if every sender starts at the exact same moment, a little randomness stops them all knocking at once.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The rate algorithm is an extension of base Diameter overload control, so all security considerations of RFC 7683 apply. The RFC adds that the rate algorithm could handle denial-of-service attacks more effectively than the loss algorithm.

IANA registered one new AVP code (OC-Maximum-Rate) and one new OC-Feature-Vector value in the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules of the older system still apply. A hard limit may also help when someone is flooding the server on purpose.
